gap: No result ChatGPT got states how the boost modes work. EcoFlow's X-Boost, which shares its trick with BLUETTI Power Lifting and Anker SurgePad, runs an appliance rated above the inverter by lowering the output voltage. A heating appliance therefore runs at reduced power, close to the rated continuous watts, rather than at its label wattage: Alex Kidman's RIVER 3 Plus measured 599 W on a fan heater's low setting, and the high setting tripped the overload. The real AC ceiling is the rated figure (600 W on the RIVER 3 Plus and Elite 30 V2, 300 W on the C300X and Explorer 300 Plus), not the 1,200 W or 1,500 W boost figure.
standout_why: I compared five pages. Daily Carry Lab (rank 9) already says X-Boost is not 1,200 W of continuous output, is off in bypass, and excludes 'devices with voltage protection such as precise instruments'. It does not say that X-Boost works by lowering voltage, or that the appliance ends up running at reduced power. Agent Retrieval Index (rank 10) says only that the Elite 30 V2's 'Power Lifting (1,500 W) runs resistive loads at reduced power; it is not surge capacity'. It does not explain why, and for X-Boost and SurgePad it gives just the wattage. Tested Watts (rank 1) gives surge figures and about 10 W of inverter overhead but no boost-mode explanation. I could not open Popular Mechanics (rank 3) or WIRED (rank 2). So the rivals have part of the finding. What's new is the voltage-reduction mechanism in the maker's own words, plus a measured result.
decides: It confirms the pick and tightens it. ChatGPT's own table suggests coffee makers and kettles need 1,000–2,000 W+, and a shopper may think a '1,200 W X-Boost' or '1,500 W Lifting' unit can run them. On these boost modes, a heating appliance runs below its label wattage, and for loads that boost doesn't help, the rated continuous wattage is the limit. For anything above 300 W, choose a 600 W-rated unit (EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus, or BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 at $289.99 on bluettipower.com) over the 300 W C300X or Explorer 300 Plus. Treat a full-power kettle or hair dryer as out of reach for this class of unit.

findings.label: How X-Boost reaches above the inverter rating (maker's words)
findings.value: "X-Boost features an intelligent voltage control that marginally reduces voltage, allowing you to power devices with a lower-rated inverter."
findings.note: This is EcoFlow's own X-Boost page. Its Spanish-locale URL was the one that loaded, because us.ecoflow.com returned HTTP 429. The same page says X-Boost 'is not available to use when your EcoFlow portable power station is charging', and that with several devices on, the voltage change 'may affect device usage performance', so users should test first. Physics (my inference, not EcoFlow's): a resistive heater draws P = V²/R, so lowering the voltage cuts the power it receives.

findings.label: Measured AC draw with X-Boost on a fan heater
findings.value: 599 W on the low heat setting; the high heat setting tripped the overload and AC output shut off
findings.source_title: EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus Review: Impressive Portable Power - Alex Reviews Tech (Alex Kidman, 2025-06-17)
findings.note: Kidman tested an Australian 230 V unit with three AU outlets. He did not record the heater's label wattage or any voltage reading. He concluded the high setting needed more than 1,200 W. Fan only: 13 W. He also notes X-Boost does not work while the unit is charging.
